name: Susa
info: Susa was an ancient city in the lower Zagros Mountains of Iran, between the Karkheh and Dez Rivers, settled from about 4200 BCE, a capital of Elam and the winter capital of the Achaemenid Empire.

facts.founded: A settlement was founded there as early as 4200 BCE, according to calibrated carbon-14 dating.
facts.where: In the lower Zagros Mountains about 250 km east of the Tigris, between the Karkheh and Dez Rivers, in Khuzestan in Iran.
facts.known: Capital of Elam; winter capital of the Achaemenid Empire; the palace of Darius; the stele of the Code of Hammurabi, carried there as plunder; the setting of the Book of Esther and of Aeschylus's The Persians; the tomb attributed to Daniel; French excavations from 1885
facts.today: The ancient centre is unoccupied, and the modern town of Shush lies to the west and north of the ruins; the site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

t: Susa was settled from about 4200 BCE, came within the Uruk cultural sphere, and became the centre of Elamite civilisation, which Mesopotamian rulers from Sargon to Ashurbanipal conquered or plundered in turn.
Cyrus the Great took it in 540 to 539 BCE, and under Darius it became one of the Achaemenid capitals, but it lost its imperial standing after Alexander and under the Seleucids.
Parthian and Sasanian kings used it as a refuge and a trading town, an Arab army took it in 642, and the Mongols razed it in 1218, after which it never regained its importance.
dyk: In about 1175 BCE the Elamite king Shutruk-Nahhunte plundered the original stele bearing the Code of Hammurabi and took it to Susa, where archaeologists found it in 1901.
ev: A settlement is founded at Susa and a monumental platform is raised
Sargon the Great incorporates Susiana into the Akkadian Empire
Shutruk-Nahhunte takes the stele of the Code of Hammurabi to Susa
Ashurbanipal of Assyria levels the city
Cyrus the Great takes Susa, which becomes part of the Achaemenid Empire
Shapur II destroys the city after a rebellion of its Christians
An Arab army under Abu Musa al-Ash'ari captures Susa

sections.origins:
Susa lay in the lower Zagros Mountains about 250 km east of the Tigris, between the Karkheh and Dez Rivers in Iran. Based on calibrated carbon-14 dating, a settlement was founded there as early as 4200 BCE, which makes Susa one of the oldest known settlements of the region. The founding corresponded with the abandonment of nearby villages, and Potts suggests that the settlement may have been founded to try to re-establish the destroyed settlement at Chogha Mish, about 25 km to the west, which had a similar massive platform.

Soon after the first settlement its inhabitants erected a monumental platform that rose over the flat surrounding landscape. Two settlements that archaeologists call the Acropolis (7 ha) and the Apadana (6.3 ha) later merged to form Susa proper (18 ha), and the Apadana was enclosed by walls of rammed earth 6 metres thick. Nearly two thousand pots of Susa I style were recovered from a cemetery near the base of the platform, most of them now in the Louvre. The painted pottery was a late, regional version of the Mesopotamian Ubaid ceramic tradition and was made carefully by hand. Copper metallurgy is also attested: as many as 40 copper axes and 10 round discs, probably mirrors, were found in the cemetery.
sections.growth:
During the Uruk period Susa came within the Uruk cultural sphere. Its remains show an imitation of the whole state apparatus of Uruk, with proto-writing, cylinder seals with Sumerian motifs and monumental architecture. Scholars dispute how far Uruk shaped the city. Holly Pittman holds that the Susanians took part entirely in an Uruk way of life, while Potts argues that Susa adopted writing and numbers only partially and selectively, and that highland influence from Khuzestan was strong as well. From about 3100 BCE Banesh pottery predominated and the Proto-Elamite tablets first appear, and Susa then became the centre of Elamite civilisation. Indus seals and etched carnelian beads found in the city from the period 2400 to 2100 BCE point to relations with the Indus Valley.

Darius the Great began a major building programme at Susa and Persepolis that included a large palace, and he recorded that the earth was dug down to rock and packed with rubble 40 and 20 cubits deep before the palace was built. Under the Seleucids the city kept its economic importance, with many merchants trading there and Charax Spasinou as its port. Under Sasanian rule the settlement extended over 400 hectares, and Susa remained a trading centre, especially for gold. It was a manufacturing centre of luxury fabrics into the Islamic period.
sections.rulers:
In the Sumerian period Susa was the capital of a state called Susiana, and control of Susiana shifted between Elam, Sumer and Akkad. Sargon the Great incorporated it into the Akkadian Empire in about 2330 BCE. Susa was an Akkadian province until about 2100 BCE, when its governor Kutik-Inshushinak rebelled and made it independent. The Third Dynasty of Ur then held it until Ur fell to the Elamites under Kindattu in about 2004 BCE, and Susa became the capital of Elam under the Shimashki dynasty. From about 1500 BCE the Anshanite kings took the title king of Anshan and Susa. Nebuchadnezzar I of Babylon plundered the city about fifty years after Shutruk-Nahhunte's raid. Assyrian rule lasted from 647 BCE until the Median capture of Susa in 617 BCE.

Cyrus the Great captured Susa between 540 and 539 BCE, and under Cambyses II it was one of four Achaemenid capitals. Its satrap surrendered to Alexander, and under the Seleucids it lost the standing of an imperial capital and became the regional capital of the satrapy of Susiana. Around 147 BCE Susa and Elymais broke away from the Seleucid Empire, and from Phraates II almost all Parthian rulers coined money there. The Roman emperor Trajan captured it briefly in 116, and it became Parthian again in 215. Ardashir I conquered it in 224, and an Arab army took it in 642.
sections.life:
Susa's main goddess was Nanaya, who had a significant temple there. Under the Middle Elamite kings the Elamite language and pantheon were imposed in Susiana, and the political and religious complex at Chogha Zanbil, 30 km south-east of the city, marked the height of that policy. The Seleucid city was named Seleucia on the Eulaeus. It is rich in Greek inscriptions, which perhaps indicate a significant number of Greeks, and large, well-equipped peristyle houses have been excavated in the royal city. It kept its Greek city-state organisation well into the Parthian period.

Susa had a Christian community in a separate district with a Nestorian bishop, the last of whom is attested in 1265, and a stucco panel with the image of a Christian saint has been found. After the Arab conquest a mosque was built, and a Jewish community with its own synagogue is recorded. Shapur II resettled the rebuilt city with prisoners of war and weavers who made silk brocade, and he renamed it Eran-Khwarrah-Shapur. The tomb attributed to the prophet Daniel stood there, and after the conquest Muslims and Christians made pilgrimages to it. Jews such as Benjamin of Tudela cited Susa as Daniel's burial place at least as early as 1167.
sections.crises:
The city was plundered and destroyed several times. Shutruk-Nahhunte and then Nebuchadnezzar I took its wealth in the 12th century BCE. In 647 BCE Ashurbanipal levelled the city during a war in which its people had fought on the other side. His inscription records that he destroyed the ziggurat, smashed its copper horns, devastated the tombs of the Elamite kings and sowed salt on the lands of Elam.

Ardashir I conquered and destroyed Susa in 224, and it was rebuilt immediately. Shapur II persecuted the Christians of the Sasanian Empire from 339, and after a rebellion of Christians in Susa he destroyed the city that year using 300 elephants. He later rebuilt it, which is believed to have followed his victory over the Romans at Amida in 359. In 642 the Arab army besieged Susa, and Muslim sources give two stories of how it fell. After entering the city the Muslims killed all the Persian nobles. They also took the treasure stored at Daniel's tomb and removed the corpse, but the caliph Umar ordered the signet ring returned and the body reburied under the riverbed.

The city recovered, but the Mongols razed it in 1218 and it never regained its previous importance. In the 15th century most of its population moved to Dezful.
sections.legacy:
Susa appears in the earliest Sumerian records, among the places obedient to Inanna in Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta. As Shushan it is named in the Hebrew Bible in Ezra, Nehemiah, Daniel and above all the Book of Esther, which is the basis of the Jewish holiday of Purim and is set in Susa. The king Ahasuerus of that book may refer to Xerxes I. Susa is also the setting of Aeschylus's The Persians of 472 BCE, the oldest surviving play in the history of theatre.

The site was examined in 1836 by Henry Rawlinson, and Marcel-Auguste Dieulafoy and Jane Dieulafoy began the first French excavations in 1885. Jacques de Morgan excavated from 1897 to 1911 and found the stele of Naram-Sin, Babylonian boundary stones, the stele bearing the Code of Hammurabi and thousands of inscribed bricks, many of which went to the Louvre. His finds showed Susa to be the most important centre of Elamite civilisation. He and his successor Roland de Mecquenem used destructive methods that damaged much of the later historical layers. Roman Ghirshman and his wife excavated the hectare-sized Ville Royale down to bare earth from 1946 to 1967, and the pottery found at its levels gave Susa a stratigraphy.

The ancient centre is unoccupied today, and the town of Shush lies west and north of the ruins. UNESCO inscribed Susa on the World Heritage List in July 2015.

summary: Susa was settled by 4200 BCE in the lower Zagros and became the capital of Elam, then a capital of the Achaemenid Empire under Darius. Seleucid, Parthian, Sasanian and Arab rulers held it, and the Mongols razed it in 1218.

END: set to 1218 (Mongol razing, 'never able to regain its previous importance'); the article adds that in the 15th century most of the population moved to Dezful, and that the modern town of Shush stands beside the unoccupied ancient centre. The editor may prefer end null or the 15th century.
START: -4200 with circa true: the article says 'as early as 4200 BC'.
Susa I is dated c. 4200-3900 BC in one place and 4200-3800 BC in the heading; I gave neither.

The 'Susa lost much of its importance' after Alexander and 'retained its importance for approximately one century' under the Seleucids are in tension in the article; I kept the loss of imperial-capital status only.
Strabo's claim that Cyrus made Susa an imperial capital is disputed in the article (no new construction); left out.
The 'Sassanid destroyed in 224' and Shapur II destroying it in 339 are as the article gives them. The article says the weavers' resettlement 'is believed' to date from after Amida in 359; hedged.
Nebuchadnezzar I's raid is 'around fifty years' after c. 1175 BCE; I wrote the relative date.
Ashurbanipal inscription is quoted by the article from a tablet found at Nineveh; I paraphrased three actions.
Event 'c. 2330 BCE' is given as 'approximately 2330 BC'. Event 540 BCE: article says between 540 and 539 BC.
Event dated 324 BCE: the mass wedding; Nearchus meeting left out. Events 339, 642 and 1218 are CE, plain years.
Left out: Islamic sources' king Shushan, Book of Jubilees, Linear Elamite details, Salvage project of 2019, population of Shush, the Shush Castle, Chogha Bonut.

Daniel's tomb: the article says the current structure largely dates to 1871; left out of the text. Muslim stories of the capture are two legendary accounts; I wrote only that sources give two stories.
The Hebrew Bible says Nehemiah lived in Susa 'during the Jews' Babylonian captivity in the 5th century BC'; left out as muddled.
